q-21207:
The normal line is vertical when the tangent to the curve is horizontal. Therefore, we require ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${x}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2{e}^{2t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t
$$

Solving ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
2t=0\,⟹\,t=0.
$$

Now, we note that

$$
{x}^{′}(0)=2{e}^{0}=2\ne 0,\,\,
$$

which confirms that the normal to the curve is indeed vertical when $t=0.$

q-15805:
First, we rearrange the equation $x-3y=2,$ as follows:

$$
y=\frac{x}{3}-\frac{2}{3}
$$

To find $x$-coordinates of the intersection points, we need to substitute $y=\frac{x}{3}-\frac{2}{3}$ into the equation of the circle and solve the resulting equation for $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y+4)^{2} & =20 \\ {x}^{2}+{(\frac{x}{3}-\frac{2}{3}+4)}^{2} & =20 \\ {x}^{2}+{(\frac{x}{3}+\frac{10}{3})}^{2} & =20 \\ {x}^{2}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{20x}{9}+\frac{100}{9} & =20 \\ \frac{10{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{20x}{9}+\frac{100}{9} & =20 \\ {x}^{2}+2x+10 & =18 \\ {x}^{2}+2x-8 & =0 \\ (x+4)(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =-4,2.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the $y$-coordinates of the intersection points, we need to substitute $x=-4,2$ into the equation of the line and compute $y$-values. Start with $x=-4$:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{x}{3}-\frac{2}{3} \\  & =-\frac{4}{3}-\frac{2}{3} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the first intersection point is $(-4,-2).$ Next, we plug in $x=2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{x}{3}-\frac{2}{3} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}-\frac{2}{3} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second intersection point is $(2,0).$

Therefore, the line $x-3y=2$ intersects the circle ${x}^{2}+(y+4)^{2}=20$ at the points $(-4,-2)$ and $(2,0).$

q-117247:
First, we rearrange the equation $x-3y=-4,$ as follows:

$$
y=\frac{x}{3}+\frac{4}{3}.
$$

To find $x$-coordinates of the intersection points, we need to substitute $y=\frac{x}{3}+\frac{4}{3}$ into the equation of the circle and solve the resulting equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2}+{y}^{2}=5 \\ (x-1)^{2}+{(\frac{x}{3}+\frac{4}{3})}^{2} & =5 \\ {x}^{2}-2x+1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{8x}{9}+\frac{16}{9} & =5 \\ \frac{10{x}^{2}}{9}-\frac{10x}{9}+\frac{25}{9} & =\frac{45}{9} \\ \frac{10{x}^{2}}{9}-\frac{10x}{9}-\frac{20}{9} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-x-2 & =0 \\ (x+1)(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =-1,2.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the $y$-coordinates of the intersection points, we need to substitute $x=-1,2$ into the equation of the line and compute $y$-values. Start with $x=-1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{x}{3}+\frac{4}{3} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}+\frac{4}{3} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the first intersection point is $(-1,1).$ Next, we plug in $x=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{x}{3}+\frac{4}{3} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}+\frac{4}{3} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second intersection point is $(2,2).$

Therefore, the line $x-3y=-4$ intersects the circle $(x-1)^{2}+{y}^{2}=5$ at the points $(2,2)$ and $(-1,1).$

q-117542:
To find $x$-coordinate of the intersection point, we need to substitute $y=-3x-11$ into the equation of the circle and solve the resulting equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y+1)^{2} & =10 \\ {x}^{2}+(-3x-11+1)^{2} & =10 \\ {x}^{2}+(-3x-10)^{2} & =10 \\ {x}^{2}+9{x}^{2}+60x+100 & =10 \\ 10{x}^{2}+60x+100 & =10 \\ 10{x}^{2}+60x+90 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+6x+9 & =0 \\ (x+3)^{2} & =0 \\ x+3 & =0 \\ x & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

To find $y$-coordinate of the intersection point, we need to substitute $x=-3$ into the equation of the line and compute $y$-value, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-3x-11 \\  & =-3(-3)-11 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the line $y=-3x-11$ intersects the circle ${x}^{2}+(y+1)^{2}=10$ at the point $(-3,-2).$

q-117546:
First, we rearrange the equation $-2x+3y=12,$ as follows:

$$
y=\frac{2x}{3}+4
$$

To find $x$-coordinates of the intersection points, we need to substitute $y=\frac{2x}{3}+4$ into the equation of the circle and solve the resulting equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2} & =13 \\ (x+1)^{2}+{(\frac{2x}{3}+4+1)}^{2} & =13 \\ (x+1)^{2}+{(\frac{2x}{3}+5)}^{2} & =13 \\ {x}^{2}+2x+1+\frac{4{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{20x}{3}+25 & =13 \\ \frac{13{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{26x}{3}+13 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+6x+9 & =0 \\ (x+3)^{2} & =0 \\ x+3 & =0 \\ x & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

q-54242:
To find $x$-coordinates of the intersection points, we need to substitute $y=-x+3$ into the equation of the circle and solve the resulting equation for $x,$ if possible:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =5 \\ (x+1)^{2}+(-x+3)^{2} & =5 \\ {x}^{2}+2x+1+{x}^{2}-6x+9 & =5 \\ 2{x}^{2}-4x+5 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

If we compute the discriminant $D$ of the above quadratic equation, then we get

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =(-4)^{2}-4\cdot 2\cdot 5 \\  & =16-40 \\  & =-24.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $D=-24<0$, there are no real solutions to the equation $2{x}^{2}-4x+5=0.$

Hence, we conclude that the circle $(x+1)^{2}+{y}^{2}=5$ does not intersect the line $y=-x+3$ at any point.

q-117737:
First, we rearrange the equation $x+2y=4,$ as follows:

$$
y=-\frac{1}{2}x+2
$$

To find $x$-coordinates of the intersection points, we need to substitute $y=-\frac{1}{2}x+2$ into the equation of the circle and solve the resulting equation for $x,$ if possible:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{2}x+2)}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-2x+4 & =1 \\ \frac{5{x}^{2}}{4}-2x+3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we compute the discriminant $D$ of the above quadratic equation, then we get

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={2}^{2}-4\cdot \frac{5}{4}\cdot 3 \\  & =4-15 \\  & =-11.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $D=-11<0$, there are no real solutions to the equation $\frac{5{x}^{2}}{4}-2x+3=0.$

Hence, we conclude that the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ does not intersect the line $x+2y=4$ at any point.

q-117859:
To find the $x$-coordinate of $A$, we set $y=0$ in the equation of the line and solve for $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}2(0)-3x & =-24 \\ -3x & =-24 \\ x & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, to find the $y$-coordinate of $B$, we set $x=0$ and solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}2y-3(0) & =-24 \\ 2y & =-24 \\ y & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $A$ and $B$ have the coordinates $(8,0)$ and $(0,-12)$, respectively.

If the segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ is a diameter of the circle, then the midpoint must be the center of the circle. Using the midpoint formula, we find that the center of the circle is at

$$
(\frac{8+0}{2},\frac{0-12}{2})=(4,-6).
$$

Now, to find the radius of the circle, we compute the distance between the center $(4,-6)$ and a point on the circle, say $A(8,0),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{(4-8)}^{2}+(-6-0)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+36} \\  & =\sqrt{52} \\  & =2\sqrt{13}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, since the circle has center $(4,-6)$ and radius $r=2\sqrt{13},$ the equation of the circle is

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-4)^{2}+(y-(-6))^{2} & ={(2\sqrt{13})}^{2} \\ (x-4)^{2}+(y+6)^{2} & =52.\end{aligned}
$$

q-78784:
To find the $x$-coordinate of $A$, we set $y=0$ in the equation of the line and solve for $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+0 & =2 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, to find the $y$-coordinate of $B$, we set $x=0$ and solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}0+y & =2 \\ y & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $A$ and $B$ have the  coordinates $(2,0)$ and $(0,2)$, respectively.

If the segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ is a diameter of the circle, then the midpoint must be the center of the circle. Using the midpoint formula, we find that the center of the circle is at

$$
(\frac{2+0}{2},\frac{0+2}{2})=(1,1).
$$

Now, to find the radius of the circle, we compute the distance between the center $(1,1)$ and a point on the circle, say $A(2,0),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{(1-2)^{2}+(1-0)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since the circle has center $(1,1)$ and radius $r=\sqrt{2},$ the equation of the circle is

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-1)}^{2}+(y-1)^{2} & ={(\sqrt{2})}^{2} \\ {(x-1)}^{2}+(y-1)^{2} & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

q-7632:
First, we must group the $x$ terms and the $y$ terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}-10x-36y & =4 \\ (5{x}^{2}-10x)+(9{y}^{2}-36y) & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must complete the square for both the $x$ and $y$ terms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(5{x}^{2}-10x)+(9{y}^{2}-36y) & =4 \\ 5[{x}^{2}-2x]+9[{y}^{2}-4y] & =4 \\ 5[(x-1)^{2}-{1}^{2}]+9[(y-2)^{2}-{2}^{2}] & =4 \\ 5[(x-1)^{2}-1]+9[(y-2)^{2}-4] & =4 \\ 5(x-1)^{2}-5+9(y-2)^{2}-36 & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rearrange the equation into the desired form:

$$
\begin{aligned}5(x-1)^{2}-5+9(y-2)^{2}-36 & =4 \\ 5(x-1)^{2}+9(y-2)^{2} & =4+5+36 \\ 5(x-1)^{2}+9(y-2)^{2} & =45 \\ \frac{(x-1)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{5} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-1)^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{(\sqrt{5})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse is centered at $(1,2).$

q-7639:
First, we must group the $x$ and $y$ terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-2x+12y & =-11 \\ ({x}^{2}-2x)+(2{y}^{2}+12y) & =-11\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we complete the square for both the $x$ and $y$ terms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}^{2}-2x)+(2{y}^{2}+12y) & =-11 \\ [{x}^{2}-2x]+2[{y}^{2}+6y] & =-11 \\ [(x-1)^{2}-{1}^{2}]+2[(y+3)^{2}-{3}^{2}] & =-11 \\ [(x-1)^{2}-1]+2[(y+3)^{2}-9] & =-11 \\ (x-1)^{2}-1+2(y+3)^{2}-18 & =-11\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rearrange the equation into the desired form:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2}-1+2(y+3)^{2}-18 & =-11 \\ (x-1)^{2}+2(y+3)^{2} & =-11+1+18 \\ (x-1)^{2}+2(y+3)^{2} & =8 \\ \frac{(x-1)^{2}}{8}+\frac{(y+3)^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-1)^{2}}{(2\sqrt{2})^{2}}+\frac{(y+3)^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Since $2\sqrt{2}>2,$ the length of the major axis is $2\cdot 2\sqrt{2}=4\sqrt{2},$ the length of the minor axis is $2\cdot 2=4,$ and the ellipse is centered at $(1,-3).$

Therefore,  I and III are true, and II is false.

q-16565:
First, we must group the $x$ terms and the $y$ terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+10x-16y+25 & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}+10x)+(4{y}^{2}-16y)+25 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we complete the square for both the $x$ and $y$ terms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}^{2}+10x)+(4{y}^{2}-16y)+25 & =0 \\ [{x}^{2}+10x]+4[{y}^{2}-4y]+25 & =0 \\ [(x+5)^{2}-{5}^{2}]+4[(y-2)^{2}-{2}^{2}]+25 & =0 \\ [(x+5)^{2}-25]+4[(y-2)^{2}-4]+25 & =0 \\ (x+5)^{2}-25+4(y-2)^{2}-16+25 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rearrange the equation into the desired form:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+5)^{2}-25+4(y-2)^{2}-16+25 & =0 \\ (x+5)^{2}+4(y-2)^{2} & =25-25+16 \\ (x+5)^{2}+4(y-2)^{2} & =16 \\ \frac{(x+5)^{2}}{16}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+5)^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Since $4>2,$ the length of the major axis is $2\cdot 4=8.$

q-16561:
First, we must group the $x$ terms and the $y$ terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}25{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+100x–40y+100 & =0 \\ (25{x}^{2}+100x)+(4{y}^{2}-40y)+100 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we complete the square for both the $x$ and $y$ terms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(25{x}^{2}+100x)+(4{y}^{2}-40y)+100 & =0 \\ 25[{x}^{2}+4x]+4[{y}^{2}-10y]+100 & =0 \\ 25[(x+2)^{2}-{2}^{2}]+4[(y-5)^{2}-{5}^{2}]+100 & =0 \\ 25[(x+2)^{2}-4]+4[(y-5)^{2}-25]+100 & =0 \\ 25(x+2)^{2}-100+4(y-5)^{2}-100+100 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rearrange the equation into the desired form:

$$
\begin{aligned}25(x+2)^{2}-100+4(y-5)^{2}-100+100 & =0 \\ 25(x+2)^{2}+4(y-5)^{2} & =-100+100+100 \\ 25(x+2)^{2}+4(y-5)^{2} & =100 \\ \frac{(x+2)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-5)^{2}}{25} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+2)^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{(y-5)^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Since $5>2,$ the length of the minor axis is $2\cdot 2=4.$

q-3397:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})(2{e}^{2x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})(2{e}^{2x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2}{3}\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2}{3}I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}J \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2}{3}(\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}-\frac{2}{3}I) \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{9}-\frac{4}{9}I \\ \frac{13}{9}I & =\frac{2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-3{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9} \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{2x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}{13}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-15422:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{6x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6{e}^{6x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$

$$

For the expansion of $\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x),$ we recall the standard result

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x) & =x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

To obtain the expansion of $\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-4x),$ we replace $x$ with $-4x$ in the standard expansion:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-4x) & =(-4x)-\frac{(-4x)^{2}}{2}+\frac{(-4x)^{3}}{3}-⋯ \\  & =-4x-8{x}^{2}-\frac{64{x}^{3}}{3}-⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, subtracting the expansion for $\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-4x)$ from the expansion for $\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1+x}{1-4x}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-4x) \\  & =(x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-⋯)-(-4x-8{x}^{2}-\frac{64{x}^{3}}{3}-⋯) \\  & =(1+4)x+(-\frac{1}{2}+8){x}^{2}+(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{64}{3}){x}^{3}+⋯ \\  & =5x+\frac{15{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{65{x}^{3}}{3}+⋯\end{aligned}
